slides.title: Pronouns
slides.text:
A **pronoun** takes the place of a noun.

**he, she, it, they, him, her, them**

“Ali is tall. **He** plays basketball.”

slides.title: The antecedent
slides.text:
The noun a pronoun stands for is called its **antecedent**.

“The dog wagged **its** tail.” → **its** stands for **the dog**.

slides.title: Make them match
slides.text:
One boy → **he / him / his**
One girl → **she / her**
One thing or animal → **it / its**
More than one → **they / them / their**

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
1. Find the pronoun.
2. Look **back** in the text for the noun it stands for.
3. Check: one or more? Boy, girl or thing? The pronoun must match.

example.explain: **They** stands for **my sisters**. Sisters = more than one, so **they** is right.

together.passage: Grandma loves her garden. ___ waters the plants every morning. The tomatoes are red and big. Grandma picks them for lunch.
together.hint: Who waters the plants? Look back at the first sentence. Is it a man, a woman, a thing, or many people?

sentences: Grandma loves her garden.
___ waters the plants every morning.
The tomatoes are red and big.
Grandma picks them for lunch.
evidence.stem: Tap the sentence that names who the pronoun stands for.
evidence.wrong: This sentence does not name the person who waters the plants. Look back to the start.

checks.passage: The birds sang. ___ were in the tree.
checks.why: **Birds** means more than one, so we use **they**.

checks.passage: Omar lost his pen. Mona found ___ under the desk.
My brother and I went to the park. ___ played football.
checks.why: “My brother and I” includes me, so the pronoun is **we**.

again.title: Point back
again.text:
Every pronoun **points back** to a noun.

Put your finger on the pronoun. Move it back until you find the noun. Do they match?
again.example: “The cats were hungry, so I fed ___.” Point back → **the cats** (more than one) → **them**.

slides.title: Agreement
slides.text:
A pronoun must **agree** with its antecedent:

1. **Number**: one, or more than one
2. **Gender**: male, female, or a thing

“The girls packed **their** bags.” Girls = more than one → their.

slides.title: Owning pronouns match too
slides.text:
**his, her, its, their** must match as well.

“The tree lost **its** leaves.” (one tree)
“The trees lost **their** leaves.” (many trees)

slides.title: Look back carefully
slides.text:
The antecedent may be a sentence or two back.

Keep track of **who or what** the text is talking about, and whether it is one or many.

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
1. Find the pronoun.
2. Find the noun it stands for, earlier in the text.
3. Check number and gender.

Point to the sentence that names the antecedent. It proves which pronoun is right.

sentences.t: Their teacher hung it on the wall.

example.explain:
**Their** stands for **the students**: more than one. **It** stands for **the project**: one thing.

Both pronouns agree.

together.passage: The camel is well suited to the desert. Its wide feet help it walk on soft sand. Thick eyelashes protect ___ eyes from blowing dust. Camels can also close their noses during sandstorms.
together.hint: Whose eyes are they? Is the text talking about one camel or many at that point?
together.good: Yes! The text is about **the camel**: one animal. So it is **its** eyes.

sentences: The camel is well suited to the desert.
Its wide feet help it walk on soft sand.
Thick eyelashes protect ___ eyes from blowing dust.
Camels can also close their noses during sandstorms.
evidence.stem: Tap a sentence that shows the eyes belong to one camel.
evidence.wrong: This sentence is about more than one camel, or does not name the owner. Find a sentence about one camel.

checks.passage: Huda and Reem brought ___ own lunches.
The bicycle had a flat tire, so Dad fixed ___.
The boys cleaned the classroom. The teacher thanked ___ for their hard work.
checks.why: The teacher thanked **the boys**: more than one → **them**.

again.title: Count and check
again.text:
1. Is the antecedent **one** or **more than one**?
2. Is it a **boy, a girl or a thing**?

Pick the pronoun that fits both answers.
again.example: “The kitten chased ___ tail.” One? Yes. An animal? Yes → **its** tail.

slides.title: Two antecedents with “and”
slides.text:
Two nouns joined by **and** need a plural pronoun.

“Sami **and** Fahad finished **their** model.”

slides.title: Two antecedents with “or” / “nor”
slides.text:
With **or** or **nor**, match the **nearer** noun.

“Either the teacher or the **students** will share **their** ideas.”

“Neither the boys nor **Ali** forgot **his** book.”

slides.title: Skip the words in between
slides.text:
“One **of the cars** lost **its** wheel.” The antecedent is **one**, not cars.

“The **basket** of oranges tipped on **its** side.” The basket tipped, not the oranges.

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
1. Find the pronoun.
2. Find the true antecedent: cross out phrases like “of the cars”.
3. Check: are nouns joined by **and**, or by **or / nor**?

Point to the words that prove what the antecedent is.

sentences.t: One of the palm trees lost its leaves in the storm.

example.explain: Cross out “of the palm trees”. The antecedent is **one** (palm tree), so **its** is correct, not “their”.

together.passage: Every year, the city holds a race for young cyclists. This year, one of the boys from our school reached the final, and ___ bike was the oldest in the race. The other riders had new, light bikes. Before the race, Majid and his coach checked the old bike carefully. They tightened the brakes and pumped up the tires. Majid finished fourth, and the crowd cheered for him.
together.hint: Cross out “of the boys from our school”. How many riders own the old bike?
together.good: Yes! The antecedent is **one** of the boys: one boy, so **his** bike.

sentences: Every year, the city holds a race for young cyclists.
This year, one of the boys from our school reached the final, and ___ bike was the oldest in the race.
The other riders had new, light bikes.
Before the race, Majid and his coach checked the old bike carefully.
They tightened the brakes and pumped up the tires.
Majid finished fourth, and the crowd cheered for him.
evidence.stem: Tap 2 sentences that show the oldest bike belonged to one boy.
evidence.wrong: This sentence does not show who owned the old bike. Find the sentences about one boy and the old bike.

checks.passage: Neither the players nor Coach Faisal forgot ___ water bottle.
checks.why: With **nor**, match the nearer noun: **Coach Faisal**, one man → **his**.

checks.passage: The box of old photographs had lost ___ lid.
checks.why: Cross out “of old photographs”. The **box** lost the lid: one thing → **its**.

checks.passage: Mona and Laila practiced ___ speeches together.

again.title: Cross out and count
again.text:
1. Cross out phrases like “of the…”.
2. Count what is left: one or more?
3. With **and** → more than one. With **or / nor** → look at the nearer noun.
again.example: “The bag of apples fell off ___ hook.” Cross out “of apples” → **the bag** = one thing → **its** hook.

slides.title: Clear reference
slides.text:
A pronoun must point to **one clear** antecedent.

“Faisal told Ahmed that **he** had won.” Who won? Unclear!

Fix: “Faisal told Ahmed, ‘You have won.’” or name the person again.

slides.title: Vague “they” and “it”
slides.text:
“**They** say the new road will open soon.” Who are they?

“The city council says the new road will open soon.” Now it is clear.

A pronoun needs a real noun to point to.

slides.title: Agreement across a passage
slides.text:
In long passages, the antecedent may be several sentences back, with other nouns in between.

Ask: which noun is the sentence really talking about? Is it one or many?

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
1. Find the pronoun.
2. List every noun before it that it could point to.
3. If two nouns fit, the reference is unclear.
4. Point to the words that name the true antecedent, and check number and gender.

sentences.t: The old map was found inside a wooden chest.
Historians said it was more than two hundred years old.

example.explain:
**It** could mean the map **or** the chest. The reader cannot be sure.

Clear version: “Historians said **the map** was more than two hundred years old.”

together.passage: Two students, Reem and Noura, entered the national science fair with a project on water filters. Reem designed the filter, while Noura tested water samples from three different wells. Each of the samples was stored in ___ own glass jar. After weeks of testing, the girls found that their filter removed most of the sand and dirt. When the judges visited their table, Reem explained the design, and Noura showed the results. The project won second prize and was later displayed at the city library.
together.stem: Which pronoun correctly completes the third sentence?
together.hint: Cross out “of the samples”. What is the true antecedent: one, or many?
together.good: Yes! The antecedent is **each**, which means one sample at a time. So: **its** own glass jar.

sentences: Two students, Reem and Noura, entered the national science fair with a project on water filters.
Reem designed the filter, while Noura tested water samples from three different wells.
Each of the samples was stored in ___ own glass jar.
After weeks of testing, the girls found that their filter removed most of the sand and dirt.
When the judges visited their table, Reem explained the design, and Noura showed the results.
The project won second prize and was later displayed at the city library.
evidence.stem: Tap the sentence that holds the antecedent of the missing pronoun.
evidence.wrong: The missing pronoun does not point to anything in this sentence. Find the sentence with the blank and its antecedent “each”.

checks.passage: When Khalid met his cousin Sami at the airport, he was very tired.
checks.why: Two men are named before “he”. The reader cannot tell which one was tired.

checks.passage: The scientists tested the new medicine on mice, and they responded well.
checks.stem: Which revision makes the reference clear?
options: The scientists tested the new medicine on mice, and it responded well.
The scientists tested it on mice, and they responded well.
They tested the new medicine on mice, and they responded well.
The scientists tested the new medicine on mice, and the mice responded well.
checks.why: “They” could mean the scientists or the mice. Naming **the mice** removes the doubt.

checks.passage: Each of the bridges in the old town has ___ own name and history.
checks.why: The antecedent is **each** (one bridge at a time), not “bridges”. One thing → **its**.

again.title: Could it be someone else?
again.text:
After every pronoun, ask: **Could it point to someone or something else?**

If yes, replace the pronoun with the noun, or rewrite the sentence.
again.example:
“Mona gave Laila her book.” Whose book? Could be either!

Clear: “Mona gave Laila **Mona's** book.” or “Mona lent her own book to Laila.”
